n: Luke opens like a careful historian. Many others had already written accounts of what Christians believed about Jesus, setting events in order.

f.g: Undertaken, attempted.
Fully established, firmly accepted.

n: Those accounts came from people who had been eyewitnesses from the start and who served as ministers of the word. Luke wasn’t an eyewitness himself, so he relied on those who were.

f.g: Servants of the message — those who preached the gospel.

n: Having researched everything carefully from the beginning, Luke decided to write an orderly account for “most excellent Theophilus” — perhaps a Roman official or a patron.

f.g: Having traced everything accurately.
Greek “friend of God” or “loved by God”; Acts is also addressed to him.

n: His purpose: so Theophilus could be sure the things he had been taught were true. Luke writes to strengthen faith with solid history.

f.g: Greek katēcheō, taught orally — the root of “catechism.”

n: The story begins in the reign of Herod the Great with a priest, Zacharias, of the priestly division of Abijah. His wife Elisabeth also descended from Aaron — a doubly priestly family.

f.g: Herod the Great, king of Judea under Rome, who died around 4 BC.
Abijah’s division — one of 24 rotating groups of priests.

n: Both were righteous in God’s eyes, faithfully keeping all the Lord’s commandments and ordinances.

f.g: Without fault in the eyes of the law — faithful, not sinless.

n: Yet they had no children, because Elisabeth couldn’t conceive, and both were old. Like Abraham and Sarah, they faced a long sorrow that God would turn into joy.

f.g: Unable to have children — often seen then as a cause of shame.
Advanced in age.

n: While Zacharias was serving his turn as priest in the temple…

f.g: Performed his priestly duties.

n: …he was chosen by lot to burn incense in the Holy Place — an honor that might come only once in a priest’s lifetime.

f.w: his lot was to burn incense
f.g: With thousands of priests, this duty was assigned by casting lots.

n: Outside, the crowd of worshippers prayed during the incense offering. Rising incense symbolized prayers rising to God.
An angel of the Lord appeared, standing at the right side of the incense altar.

f.g: A small gold altar just before the veil of the Holy of Holies.

n: Zacharias was startled and overcome with fear.
The angel said: don’t be afraid; your prayer has been heard. Elisabeth will bear you a son, and you will name him John.

f.g: From Hebrew Yohanan, “the Lord is gracious.”

n: He will bring you joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth.
He will be great before the Lord, will drink no wine or strong drink, and will be filled with the Holy Ghost even before birth.
He will turn many Israelites back to the Lord their God.
He will go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, turning hearts of fathers to children and the disobedient to wisdom, to prepare a people ready for the Lord.

f.w: a people prepared for the Lord

n: Zacharias asked for proof: how can I be sure? I’m old, and so is my wife. His question focused on obstacles rather than God’s promise.
The angel revealed himself: “I am Gabriel, who stands in God’s presence,” sent with good news. Latter-day Saints understand Gabriel to be Noah.

f.g: Hebrew “God is my strength.”
Good news — the same word as “gospel.”

n: Because he didn’t believe, Zacharias would be unable to speak until the promise came true — a sign and a gentle discipline.

f.g: Unable to speak.

n: Meanwhile the people outside wondered why he was taking so long in the temple.

f.g: Stayed, delayed.

n: When he came out, he couldn’t speak or give the usual blessing. He made signs with his hands, and they realized he had seen a vision.

f.g: Made signs, gestured.

n: When his week of temple service ended, he went home to the hill country.

f.g: Service, period of duty.

n: Afterward Elisabeth became pregnant and stayed in seclusion for five months.
She praised God: the Lord has looked on me with favor and taken away my public disgrace of childlessness.

f.g: Shame, disgrace.

n: Six months into Elisabeth’s pregnancy, God sent Gabriel to Nazareth, a small, overlooked village in Galilee.

f.g: A small hill village in lower Galilee.

n: He came to a virgin named Mary, engaged to Joseph, a descendant of King David.

f.g: Betrothed — a binding engagement, legally like marriage, before the couple lived together.

n: Gabriel greeted her: “Rejoice, you who are highly favored! The Lord is with you.” Mary was chosen by grace.

f.g: A greeting meaning “rejoice” or “greetings.”
Greatly graced by God.

n: Mary was troubled and thoughtfully wondered what such a greeting could mean. She pondered before reacting.

f.g: Considered, reasoned out.

n: The angel reassured her: don’t be afraid, Mary; you have found favor with God.
She would conceive and give birth to a son, and name him Jesus.

f.g: Greek form of Hebrew Yeshua (Joshua), “the Lord saves.”

n: He would be great, called Son of the Most High, and given the throne of his ancestor David — fulfilling God’s covenant with David.

f.w: the throne of his father David

n: He would reign over Jacob’s house forever; his kingdom would never end.

f.w: of his kingdom there shall be no end

n: Mary asked how this could happen, since she was a virgin. Unlike Zacharias, she wasn’t asking for proof but for understanding.

f.g: I have not had relations with a man.

n: The Holy Ghost would come upon her and the power of the Most High would overshadow her, so the holy child would be called the Son of God. Jesus’ divine Father is God himself.
As a sign, Gabriel shared that Mary’s relative Elisabeth, once called barren, was now six months pregnant in her old age.

f.g: Relative, kinswoman — the exact relationship is unknown.

n: For nothing is impossible with God.

f.w: with God nothing shall be impossible

n: Mary answered with complete trust: “I am the Lord’s servant. Let it be as you have said.” A model of faithful submission.

f.g: Female servant.

f.w: be it unto me according to thy word

n: Soon after, Mary hurried to a town in the hill country of Judea.

f.g: Judah, the southern region around Jerusalem.

n: She entered Zacharias’s home and greeted Elisabeth.

f.g: Greeted.

n: When Elisabeth heard Mary’s greeting, her unborn baby leaped, and she was filled with the Holy Ghost. Even before birth, John responded to Christ.
She exclaimed loudly: blessed are you among women, and blessed is the child you carry!

f.g: The child she was carrying.

n: Humbly she asked why she should be honored with a visit from the mother of her Lord. By the Spirit, she already knew who Mary’s child was.
As soon as she heard Mary’s voice, her baby leaped for joy.
Blessed is the woman who believed that the Lord’s promises to her would be fulfilled — a contrast to Zacharias’s doubt.

f.g: Fulfillment.

n: Mary’s song of praise, the “Magnificat,” begins: my soul magnifies the Lord — declares his greatness. It echoes Hannah’s song in 1 Samuel.

f.g: Make great, glorify. “Magnificat” is the Latin first word of this song.

f.w: My soul doth magnify the Lord

n: Her spirit rejoices in God her Savior. Even the mother of Jesus needed a Savior.
God noticed the humble status of his servant; from now on every generation will call her blessed.

f.g: Humble condition.

f.w: all generations shall call me blessed

n: The Mighty One has done great things for her; his name is holy.
God’s mercy extends to every generation of those who reverence him.

f.g: Hold him in reverent awe and respect.

n: Mary speaks of God’s acts as already done. His powerful arm scatters those who are proud in their thoughts.

f.g: A Hebrew image for God’s power in action.

n: He brings down rulers from their thrones and lifts up the lowly. God reverses the world’s order.
He fills the hungry with good things and sends the rich away empty.
He has helped his servant Israel, remembering his mercy.

f.g: Helped.

n: Just as he promised Abraham and his descendants forever. The birth of Jesus fulfills the Abrahamic covenant.

f.w: to Abraham, and to his seed for ever

n: Mary stayed about three months — likely until John’s birth — then returned home.

f.g: Stayed, remained.

n: Elisabeth’s time came, and she gave birth to a son.

f.g: Give birth.

n: Neighbors and relatives heard of the Lord’s great mercy to her and celebrated with her.
On the eighth day they gathered to circumcise the baby and expected to name him Zacharias after his father.

f.g: Circumcision, the sign of the covenant, was performed on the eighth day.

n: Elisabeth objected: “No, he will be called John.”
They protested that no one in the family had that name. Names usually honored relatives.
They made signs to Zacharias to ask what he wanted — suggesting he may have been deaf as well as mute.
He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” Everyone was amazed. His obedience was now complete.

f.g: A wooden tablet coated with wax for writing.

n: Immediately he could speak again, and his first words praised God.
Awe fell on the neighbors, and these events became the talk of all the Judean hill country.

f.g: Talked about widely.

n: Everyone who heard kept wondering, “What will this child become?” The Lord’s hand was clearly with him.

f.w: laid them up in their hearts
f.g: Remembered and pondered them.

n: Filled with the Holy Ghost, Zacharias prophesied. His song is called the “Benedictus,” from its first Latin word.

f.g: Spoke by inspiration.

n: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who has come to his people and redeemed them. Zacharias speaks of redemption as already accomplished, so certain is it.

f.g: Came to help — God’s saving presence.
Bought back, freed by paying a price.

n: God has raised up a mighty Savior from David’s family. The “horn” symbolizes strength, like a powerful animal’s horns.

f.g: A mighty Savior; horns symbolize power.

n: Just as he promised through his holy prophets from the beginning of the world.
He promised to save us from our enemies and all who hate us.
He has shown the mercy promised to our ancestors and remembered his holy covenant.
The oath he swore to our father Abraham.
That, rescued from our enemies, we could serve him without fear…
…in holiness and righteousness all our lives. The goal of salvation isn’t only rescue but a holy life of service.
Turning to his baby, Zacharias prophesies: you will be called the prophet of the Most High, going before the Lord to prepare his way.
John would teach people how to be saved through the forgiveness of their sins.
All because of God’s tender mercy, by which the sunrise from heaven has come to us — a beautiful name for the Messiah.

f.g: Dawn, sunrise — a title for Christ as the rising light.

n: He will shine on those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death and guide our feet into the way of peace.
John grew and became strong in spirit and lived in the wilderness until he began his public ministry to Israel. Modern revelation adds that he was ordained by an angel when eight days old.

f.g: Grew, became.
